articles.title_orig: Tennessee Inmate in Critical Condition After ‘Torturous’ Botched Execution, Lawyer Says
articles.title_zh: Tennessee Inmate in Critical Condition After ‘Torturous’ Botched Execution, Lawyer Says
articles.content_orig:
After a flurry of eleventh-hour litigation, Christa Pike was strapped to a gurney Wednesday night, set to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in 200 years.
But after being injected with two ostensibly lethal doses of pentobarbital, Pike was still alive, snoring loudly as journalists selected to witness the execution glanced at one another, wondering what was happening.
“None of it was normal,” said Catherine Sweeney, a reporter for WPLN. “I covered all the executions last year, and most of the ones this year. We haven’t seen anything like it. It went really poorly.”
Pike is in critical condition and receiving life-saving medical care, her legal team said Thursday afternoon. Attorney Randy Spivey called for the governor to commute her sentence, saying she had endured punishment “greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty.”
The failure to execute Pike – who was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer – raises serious questions about what went wrong during the execution and what happens next.
Gov. Bill Lee, a Republican, announced he would call off the state’s last remaining execution this year while a third-party review takes place to “determine what exactly occurred” in Pike’s case, according to The Associated Press.
“The Governor has appropriately called for an investigation,” the office of Tennessee Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti said in a statement. “We need to know what happened.”
It’s the second such order of Lee’s tenure: He similarly paused executions in 2022, when he said he learned the proper procedure for testing the lethal drugs had not been followed.
Tennessee governor halts executions after Christa Pike survives lethal injection attempt
This was just the latest blunder by a state that has pushed ahead with executions after several years of troubles, including a failed execution attempt earlier this year . In the wake of the failure, critics of the death penalty called for a halt to executions, not just in Tennessee but in the 27 states that still practice the death penalty .
“The state of Tennessee has shown the world it cannot be trusted to implement capital punishment in a way that preserves human dignity and the rule of law,” Laura Porter, executive director of the US Campaign to End the Death Penalty, said in a statement. “This has to stop now.”
Tennessee is not alone. Multiple states have struggled with lethal injections in recent years, giving rise to novel methods, like executions by nitrogen gas , and the return of old methods, such as the firing squad .
The central issue with lethal injection is it’s a “Frankenstein version” of a medical procedure, said Corinna Barrett Lain, a professor at the University of Richmond School of Law and author of the 2025 book “Secrets of the Killing State: the Untold Story of Lethal Injection.”
These executions generally feature drugs of questionable quality, nonmedical personnel administering the drugs and patients with notoriously weak veins, Lain said. Lethal injection’s “botch rate” is twice that of other methods, she said.
“It has all of the delicacy and need for accuracy of the medical model, but then it’s been warped to suit the executioner’s needs,” she said. “It’s a recipe for disaster from the start.”
In a statement, Pike’s legal team pointed to several possible issues.
“Tonight the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution,” attorneys Spivey and Kelly Gleason said in a statement. “We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms. Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy.”
Pike was initially scheduled to be executed on Wednesday morning, but last-minute legal appeals delayed the execution to later in the day .
Tori Gessner of WKRN, one of the media witnesses, provided a detailed timeline of Pike’s execution.
The witnesses were taken into the witness chamber at 6:41 p.m., she said. The blinds that look into the execution chamber were opened at 7:26 p.m., and Pike then gave her final statement, she said. At 7:34 p.m., Pike said her arm felt like it was about to burst and she appeared to be talking, breathing, moaning and snoring over the following minutes, Gessner said.
The blinds to the room were closed at 7:46 p.m. and then reopened at 7:49 p.m., Gessner said. Pike was snoring with her mouth open at this point. The blinds then went down at 8:05 p.m., and remained closed until the witnesses were escorted out of the area at 8:53 p.m., Gessner said.
These cases pose hard questions about the US capital punishment system
Pike’s attorneys offered several other details Thursday. The execution team spent an hour trying to establish an IV line and used at least seven needles in her left arm, Spivey said.
“I’m haunted by last night,” he said. “What I saw last night is not something that should ever, ever happen again.”
Another attorney, Stephen Ferrell, said no one on her legal team has seen her and he declined to speculate about what she is experiencing.
Pike’s biggest fear “was not a fear of dying. It was a fear of prolonged, painful, traumatic death,” Ferrell said. “That’s what happened, minus the death.”
The media witnesses said they had little sense of what exactly was happening.
“I cannot emphasize enough how much of whatever just happened, happened behind a closed curtain when Christa Pike was still alive,” said Steven Hale, a reporter for the Nashville Banner.
John North, a journalist for WBIR, echoed that sentiment.
“Obviously, we have a lot of questions about what we saw and what we did not see, because there were moments when the blinds were down for us and there were moments when the blinds were up for us,” he said.
“It appeared that this did not go like they thought it was supposed to go,” he added.
The Tennessee Department of Correction said it acted according to its protocol throughout the failed execution.
“The Tennessee Department of Correction followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office,” the department said in a statement. “The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening. Christa Pike has been transported to an off-site medical facility.”
Tennessee’s lethal injection execution protocol is laid out in a 44-page document created by the Department of Correction, according to a copy obtained by the Death Penalty Information Center. CNN has requested a copy of the protocol from the Tennessee Department of Correction.
The step-by-step protocol is used to “ensure the humane and constitutional execution of inmates sentenced to death” and prohibits officials from straying from the procedure.
“There will be no deviation from the Protocol except by order of the Commissioner,” the protocol states.
The protocol approves only a one-drug method of lethal injection, specifically pentobarbital, a barbiturate that can cause death. The protocol states 100 ml of a 50 mg/ml solution of pentobarbital (a total of 5 grams) shall be checked to verify its contents and expiration dates 30 days before a scheduled execution.
The document lays out procedures leading up to, during and after the execution. Personnel prepare the primary 100 ml dose of pentobarbital solution in syringes, as well as a backup set “if the inmate is not deceased,” the protocol states.
There is no protocol for what happens if that second set does not work.
There is only limited precedent for what comes next. articles.title_zh: Gypsy Rose Blanchard’s fiancé Ken Urker dead at 33
articles.content_orig:
Gypsy Rose Blanchard’s fiancé, Ken Urker, has died.
Urker was found unresponsive at a home in Louisiana on his birthday, TMZ reported Thursday.
According to the outlet, Urker was discovered by a family member after he didn’t respond when Gypsy Rose texted him “happy birthday.”
Gypsy Rose and Urker shared their daughter, 1-year-old Aurora Raina, who was born in December 2024 .
A month before Aurora’s birth, the convicted murderer confirmed once and for all that Urker was the father of her baby — not her ex-husband, Ryan Anderson.
“There’s been a lot of chatter around the paternity of our baby and while we’ve known for sure from the beginning, I feel that it’s finally time to put all these theories to rest,” she wrote in a since-deleted post. “Ken is the father.”
“Ken is going to be an incredible dad and we are so excited to welcome our baby girl into the world,” she added.
Start your day with Page Six Daily.
Gypsy Rose and Urker met as prison pen pals in 2017 while she was behind bars for her role in the 2015 murder of her mother, Clauddine “Dee Dee” Blanchard .
They got engaged in October 2018, but they broke up in August 2019.
Gypsy Rose then married Anderson in July 2022 while still in prison, but the two split in March 2024 , just three months after she was released from prison.
Their divorce was finalized later that year.
Gypsy Rose subsequently rekindled her romance with Urker .
Just weeks after her split from Anderson, Gypsy Rose got matching husky dog tattoos with Urker.
Gypsy Rose shared a TMI confession in an April 2025 episode of “Life After Lock Up” about how “adventurous” she and Urker were in the bedroom since their reconciliation.
“Our first weekend that we reconnected, it was like a floodgate,” she shared on her Lifetime reality show.
“And naturally, now there are times that I think is harder because of schedules and business and work and, like, I want that back for us,” she added.
While showing off some of their kinky items — like a pair of fuzzy handcuffs — Gypsy Rose shared, “I’m the most adventurous girlfriend that he’s had, so I’m the freak.”

articles.title_orig: Letitia James appointed special prosecutor in alleged gang-rape at Cornell
articles.title_zh: Letitia James appointed special prosecutor in alleged gang-rape at Cornell
articles.content_orig:
New York attorney general brought in by governor after recent questions raised over university’s 2024 investigation
Kathy Hochul, the New York governor, said on Thursday she is appointing Letitia James, the state’s attorney general, as special prosecutor to investigate the alleged gang-rape at Cornell University.
“The young woman at the center of this case deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued,” Hochul said in a statement . “This action will ensure that the matter is fully and thoroughly investigated without conflict or bias, and handled independently with the rigor that this matter demands.”
In her statement, Hochul said the decision by Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins county ⁠district attorney, not to prosecute the 2024 case, and the questions raised in recent days over the Cornell police department’s investigation of the allegations, have “undercut my faith, and the public’s faith, in the district attorney’s ability to effectively investigate and prosecute the case at this time”.
Hochul said James would oversee the investigation and, if warranted, present evidence to a grand jury.
The former Cornell University student who alleges she was gang-raped at a fraternity in 2024 filed a lawsuit in September, in a case that has sparked national outrage, roiled the Ivy League campus and raised questions about why no criminal case was brought.
Van Houten declined at the time of the alleged assault to bring criminal charges, but this week said he would reopen the investigation based on new information in the woman’s lawsuit, which identifies her only by the pseudonym Jane Doe.
He has maintained that the woman’s first account to police did not include allegations that she was drugged, incapacitated beyond the ability to consent or forced into sex. After CBS News this week revealed details from the police interview transcript, he told the network he’d never seen her detailed account and had relied instead on a statement written by a campus police officer and signed by the accuser.
She is suing seven men whom she said perpetrated the assault, as well as the university, the fraternity and others.
Lawyers for two of the men she is suing have denied they perpetrated a sexual assault. One said his client had not touched the woman or engaged in any drug use.
Cornell has said it suspended the Chi Phi fraternity indefinitely and disciplined or expelled some students, but the university has declined to provide specifics, citing student privacy rules.
Under pressure from the public and politicians, including Hochul, Cornell, a private university, agreed on Wednesday to bring in outside lawyers to independently investigate how it handled the woman’s allegations.

articles.title_orig: Judge reinstates U.S. attorney in Western WA who was fired by Trump
articles.title_zh: Judge reinstates U.S. attorney in Western WA who was fired by Trump
articles.content_orig:
The ruling is the latest in the administration's battle over U.S. attorneys.
A federal judge on Thursday ordered a U.S. attorney from Western Washington who was fired by President Donald Trump in July to immediately be reinstated to the position, and is barring the Justice Department from again attempting to replace him.
The ruling from U.S. District judge Stanley Bastian is the latest escalation in the Trump administration's battle with the judiciary over DOJ efforts to install U.S. attorneys around the country without Senate confirmation.
Federal judges appointed Rogoff to the post that oversees federal prosecutions in Seattle in July, and he was fired by President Trump through an email roughly an hour later.
Rogoff then filed suit citing similar cases around the country where the Trump administration had unsuccessfully sought to install attorneys and extend their service indefinitely, which judges appointed by both parties have ruled clearly violates the appointment statute .
The Justice Department said it disagrees with the decision and plans to appeal and seek a stay.
Judge Bastian ruled from the bench in Thursday's proceeding granting Rogoff's request for a preliminary injunction -- and further enjoined Attorney General Todd Blanche and the Executive Office of the President from taking any further moves to effectuate his termination.

A San Antonio-area man is accused of planning a violent attack on the Texas State Capitol in Austin, according to a news release from the Texas Department of Public Safety (DPS).
The agency said it received credible information on Tuesday that 40-year-old Benny Caldera Jr. was planning the attack for Thursday, Oct. 1. DPS said it worked with the FBI and local partners to arrest Caldera at his home in the town of Converse.
According to court documents, on Sept. 29, Caldera allegedly told another individual that he was going to the Capitol and would "shoot it up," specifically expressing his anger toward the American Israeli Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC).
A criminal complaint alleges that Caldera said of AIPAC, "These people have to be exterminated." The complaint also alleges that Caldera stated in a recorded conversation that he had made up his mind and had said goodbye to his parents.
During the search of his home, Texas DPS Criminal Investigation Division agents allegedly found a .357 revolver loaded with six rounds and a 12-gauge shotgun in his master bedroom closet, along with six 9mm rounds. The criminal complaint alleges that the serial number on the side of the revolver frame appeared to have been filed off.
The arrest happened at 3 a.m. Wednesday, the agency said. Caldera is charged with making a terroristic threat against a public servant and charged federally for possessing a firearm with an obliterated serial number.
Caldera was released from the Bexar County Jail into federal custody on Wednesday, where he will remain, according to Texas DPS. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.
Texas DPS said its leadership team notified state lawmakers about the threat and arrest earlier in the day on Wednesday, and that the Capitol building remained open for regular operating hours. The agency said it will continue to have an increased posture at the Texas Capitol to protect all employees, visitors and state officials.

articles.title_orig: FBI arrests Massachusetts man on charge of stalking conservative podcaster Katie Miller
articles.title_zh: FBI arrests Massachusetts man on charge of stalking conservative podcaster Katie Miller
articles.content_orig:
The FBI on Thursday arrested a man on a charge of stalking former Trump administration adviser Katie Miller, an administration official familiar with the investigation told NBC News.
John Anthony Proia III, 41, was arrested and charged with stalking over allegations that he called, texted and left voicemails with “disturbing messages” about the victim, who was described as a former political adviser, and her husband, who is currently a high-level federal government employee, the Justice Department said in a news release.
The Justice Department did not name Katie Miller, though an administration official familiar with the investigation confirmed to NBC News that the victim is Miller, who is married to White House deputy chief of staff for policy Stephen Miller and hosts a popular conservative podcast.
“Thank you Todd Blanche, Leah Foley, and the FBI Washington Field Office for keeping me and my family safe. Good to see a Boston grand jury indict this man,” Miller wrote Thursday on X , referring to Attorney General Todd Blanche and U.S. Attorney Leah Foley.
Proia was indicted by a federal grand jury in Boston on Thursday on one count of cyberstalking after being arrested earlier in the day. He is alleged to have contacted the former political adviser more than 40 times in less than two months, according to the Justice Department.
The defendant is also accused of sending disturbing messages to Miller’s parents during the August-to-September time frame cited in court documents.
“As alleged in the Indictment, the defendant repeatedly and relentlessly targeted the victim, her husband and her family with deeply disturbing communications that profoundly disrupted their lives,” Foley said in a statement.
Ted Docks, special agent in charge of the FBI’s Boston Division, wrote in a statement on Thursday that Proia was arrested “for allegedly engaging in a sustained campaign of harassment to frighten this victim and her family, inflicting significant emotional distress.”
Proia made the calls, sent text messages and left voicemails from “an ever-changing series of unfamiliar phone numbers” to Miller, who lives in the Washington, D.C., area, the DOJ said.
The department added that those phone numbers were obtained through applications that provide free phone numbers for calling and messaging via Voice over Internet Protocol. The applications allow a user to hide their identity and easily generate new phone numbers, according to court filings.
According to court documents, Miller sometimes received multiple communications from Proia in one day, including calls made late at night. Miller did answer some of the calls, but Proia also left voicemails, the DOJ said.
The calls “were allegedly made by what appeared to be a male caller employing a menacing tone and often using expletives,” the Justice Department said.
The Justice Department also detailed some text messages sent to phone numbers associated with Miller’s parents.
One message Proia is alleged to have written to Miller’s mother called Stephen Miller “evil” and Katie Miller a “creature.” Another message was said to feature a photo of Katie Miller, while another read, “My god, how can you be proud of this filth?”
In a text message to the victim’s father, Proia is alleged to have written, “Hey [first name of victim’s father], how goes it? Hope your daughter marrying a Jewish Nazi/white supremacist is working out for you and [first name of victim’s mother]. Did you raise her to be trash or did that just happen naturally?”
Proia’s arrest comes after Bloomberg reported over the weekend that two senior FBI officials in Washington were demoted and reassigned to FBI headquarters due to concerns that the agency was not moving efficiently enough to investigate threatening phone calls made to Miller, three people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg.
Darren Cox, assistant director in charge the FBI’s Washington Field Office, told Bloomberg in a statement that the move was a personnel decision made at the field office level based on “our constant evaluation of mission needs.”
Michael Kosnar is the Justice Department Producer for NBC News.
Kyla Guilfoil is a breaking news reporter on the politics team for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: France school protests escalate into ‘urban violence’ as PM calls crisis cabinet meeting
articles.title_zh: France school protests escalate into ‘urban violence’ as PM calls crisis cabinet meeting
articles.content_orig:
About 900 demonstrations, blockades and related incidents under way outside high schools around the country
A fast-growing protest by high-school students over long hours, teacher shortages and decaying facilities has escalated into “urban violence”, the French government has warned, as it said many schools would switch to online classes to protect teachers and pupils.
The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, called a crisis cabinet meeting on Thursday and told ministers to cancel travel plans to deal with the demonstrations, which erupted in the Paris region last week but have snowballed across the country.
Lecornu’s office said: “This upsurge in violence makes it virtually impossible to maintain the continuity of public education and is exposing staff and students to danger.” The education minister, Édouard Geffray, is to meet pupil representatives on Friday.
About 900 demonstrations, blockades and related incidents were under way outside high schools around the country, police said, with more than 160 shut down as a result. Access was also blocked to about 30 university campuses on Thursday, including in Paris and Marseille.
Nearly 3,000 lycée students – aged between 15 and 18 – have been detained since the start of the protests, including 1,949 on Thursday alone, the interior ministry said. More than 300 police and dozens of firefighters, teachers and pupils have been injured.
The pupils’ grievances range from overloaded timetables and overcrowded classes to insufficient teachers and unbearable temperatures during heatwaves earlier this year. Riot police have been deployed to confront the increasingly violent protests.
Injuries have mainly been from hurled objects but also from police-fired riot-control projectiles, with the interior ministry announcing an internal police investigation after accusations of excessive force and brutality by officers against three pupils.
Rubbish bins have been set on fire outside many schools and more serious arson attempts have been reported inside some buildings. Fire damage in one school in Nantes in the north-west was so extensive that it will stay closed for a month, authorities said.
In the northern city of Caen, 16-year-old Maelle said she wished those setting bins on fire would protest “with words”. Students were protesting “against this government that doesn’t invest in heating, air conditioning, or teachers’ salaries”, she told AFP.
In Strasbourg in the north-east, tram services were temporarily suspended to “restrict the movements of rioters and demonstrators”, the regional prefect said, after protesting students obstructed the tracks with crowd control barriers.
“There are 35 of us per classroom,” one 17-year-old Strasbourg student said. “There aren’t enough toilets, and there are water leaks in some rooms. The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There’s zero budget, zero resources.”
Several bin fires were also reported in the southern city of Toulouse; while in Lille, young people wearing black hoodies destroyed a bus stop. In Marseille, there were attempts to light fires inside two schools. In one, a teacher was splashed with petrol.
While many teachers and several headteachers have reported being physically threatened and sometimes attacked, some support their pupils. Juliette Estiville, a high-school Spanish teacher in Paris, said that the police response had disgusted her.
“I’m actually here just to provide protection, to form a barrier between the police and the students,” she said. “Today went well, it’s going well, but I think that the teachers who come to the blockades are really there to protect our young people.”
The government has accused the radical left La France Insoumise (LFI) party of encouraging the protests, with several LFI MPs and mayors, including Bally Bagayoko, the LFI mayor of the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis, cheered at demonstrations.
The party’s candidate for the 2027 presidential election, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, insisted on Thursday that LFI backed “non-violent methods of struggle” and added that his “greatest worry is an unbearable level of police violence against these young people”.

articles.content_orig:
On Wednesday night, the Dallas Cowboys made a move that would at least temporarily boost their injury-decimated secondary when they traded with the Pittsburgh Steelers for cornerback Joey Porter Jr.
The Cowboys sent Pittsburgh a conditional 2027 sixth-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick in exchange for Porter, who had been seeking a contract extension with the Steelers since the offseason. Per ESPN, Porter must be on the gameday roster for two contests this season for the 2027 pick to go through.
It might be seen as a risk for the Cowboys to give up a second-round pick without having a contract in place for Porter. A source with knowledge of the situation told Newsweek that Dallas made the move for Porter in a bid to win this season. Owner Jerry Jones has ambitions to win the Super Bowl with this team, and the secondary needed an immediate fix amid a 1-2 start.
The Cowboys are not concerned about signing Porter to a new deal at this point in the season and have not offered the 2023 second-round pick a contract extension.
"The Cowboys have no interest in doing a deal until (Porter gets) on the field (to) see how good he is," the source said.
The Cowboys would be fine if they only had Porter as a one-year loaner for the remainder of this season, and Dallas is not believed to be planning to use the franchise tag on Porter or receiver George Pickens in 2027. However, that could change depending on how the two athletes play through the entirety of this season.
More News: Exclusive: Breakout NFL Executives Who Could Become Future General Managers
More News: 4 QBs Generating Serious Trade Buzz Weeks Before NFL Regular Season Starts
Per Pro Football Talk, if Dallas were to let Porter walk into free agency in 2027, the Cowboys would be set to receive a compensatory third-round pick in 2028 (closer to the start of the fourth round than the start of the third).
In a worst-case scenario where Porter does not agree to a new deal with Dallas, the Cowboys view the trade as giving up a second-round pick for a compensatory third while gaining one of the top coverage cornerbacks in the league this fall.
The Cowboys will enter the 2027 offseason with plenty of decisions to make about their roster. Dallas will have 20 players set to enter unrestricted free agency; six of those, including Porter and Pickens, are represented by David Mulugheta of Athletes First.
Dallas is in a better position to agree to a new deal with Porter than Pittsburgh. Per multiple reports , the heart of the dispute between Porter and the Steelers had to do with the guarantees in the deal. The Cowboys are more cash-rich than Pittsburgh and give more money guaranteed, more cash, and more signing bonus.
Another key factor that can help Porter is that the Cowboys, unlike the Steelers, have no state income taxes. Dallas can offer a higher signing bonus, which is not subject to state taxes. That will benefit Porter through the rest of this season as his game checks in Dallas won't be dinged for state taxes.

articles.title_orig: 'They’ll be hit very hard': Trump sends 9,000 troops to the Middle East after warning Iran strikes
articles.title_zh: 'They’ll be hit very hard': Trump sends 9,000 troops to the Middle East after warning Iran strikes
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. military is dispatching roughly 9,000 troops aboard a group of ships to the Middle East, a U.S. official said Thursday. The bolstering of the American military presence comes as President Donald Trump warned anew that new strikes against Iran could be on the horizon.
The troop movement, which includes a third aircraft carrier, underscores the rapidly evolving dynamic of Trump’s war against Iran as he ponders his next move, with midterm elections in the United States looming large and new signs that the nature of the conflict may be becoming more complex.
Trump has threatened that a post-midterm election escalation — despite his initial promises to Americans of a campaign that would last a matter of weeks — remains a viable option. Further complicating matters, Trump told reporters Thursday that early indications suggest that Iran is linked to the FlyDubai co-pilot who stabbed his captain and tried to crash an Israel-bound flight on Wednesday.
In an exchange with reporters at the White House, Trump raised the connection when asked by a reporter if there were any links between the pilot behind the attack and Tehran.
“I would say the answer, based on what I’m hearing, is ‘yes,’ but we’re working on it right now,” Trump said, without offering details.
Trump added that if the link to Iran is established, the United States would retaliate. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed in a Fox News interview earlier Thursday that investigators believe the FlyDubai suspect underwent “Islamist, radical indoctrination” but did not provide further details.
“Oh, they’ll be hit very hard, don’t worry,” Trump said. “You just ask them. They know what happened. They’ll be hit very hard.”
Meanwhile, the group of ships now en route to the Middle East together carry over 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines.
It includes the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group, which recently deployed with the cruiser USS Chosin, and the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group, which includes the USS John P. Murtha and USS Anchorage amphibious landing ships.
It could mean that three carriers are in the region as early as the end of October, according to the U.S. official, who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military operations.
Given the personnel already in place in the Middle East, the move would bring the U.S. naval presence to an unusually high number of more than 20,000 sailors and Marines as well as hundreds of aircraft. The Navy previously had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April for the first time since 2003.
The carriers USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington are in the region now, along with the USS Boxer amphibious readiness group. The Washington is typically deployed to the Pacific Ocean, but it was moved to the Middle East to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln, whose arduous deployment resulted in the crew being at sea for more than 260 days straight.
Trump, in a Time magazine interview published Thursday, also raised the prospects of new strikes, saying it is “possible” that he will ramp up bombing in Iran after the Nov. 3 elections in the United States.
When pressed, Trump said he could not go into further detail about his strategy.
“I can’t tell you that because look, you know, you’re asking, where are you going to bomb?” Trump said.
He said in the interview, conducted Monday, that he rejected the latest ceasefire proposal from Iran because “things that I wouldn’t have approved a year ago I wouldn’t have today.”
Trump cited as an example an offer from Iran to “open up” the Strait of Hormuz, the key energy shipping corridor, but said the overall proposal was “not good enough.”
Asked if the increasingly unpopular war would threaten Republican Party chances in November, Trump at first responded, “It’s possible.” But then he added, “It should help, because Iran will not have a nuclear weapon.”
The president said “100% of the people” oppose Iran having nuclear attack capabilities “including worldwide.”
“So, when you say it that way, it would help,” Trump added. “If you don’t say that, it could hurt.”
Yet, there’s also growing concern that Tehran might be turning to asymmetrical tactics following the FlyDubai attack and another suspicious incident in the U.K.
Authorities believe that Iran might be looking to shift strategy just as the U.S. finds greater success in loosening Iran’s grip over the Strait of Hormuz and getting Gulf allies’ oil to market, while a Navy blockade is shutting down Iran’s own oil exports.
British authorities announced on Thursday the arrest of a dual U.K.-Iranian national on suspicion of plotting a terror attack following a security incident at a U.S.-run military air base in England that British authorities have linked to Tehran .
The arrest of the 27-year-old man in Central London came after U.K. authorities arrested five men, all British nationals in their 20s and from London, in the early hours of Sunday on suspicion of explosives and terror offenses close to the RAF Fairford air base
The base has been used by American bombers to strike Iran. The suspects have since been released on bail .
Madhani reported from Jerusalem. Associated Press writers Seung Min Kim and Will Weissert in Washington contributed to this report.

China’s major refiners have suspended most refined fuel exports for October as Beijing prioritizes domestic supply security, removing another source of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel from an already severely constrained global market.
PetroChina has cancelled several gasoline and jet fuel cargoes scheduled for October, while Zhejiang Petrochemical did not schedule exports during China’s week-long National Day holiday, Reuters reported, citing four people familiar with the matter. Beijing has yet to authorize October exports outside Hong Kong and Macau, although shipments could resume after the holiday ends on October 7 depending on domestic inventories and refinery output.
The move follows a sharp deterioration in China’s own fuel-stock position. Kpler estimates commercial diesel and gasoil inventories are around 20 million barrels below pre-war levels, while gasoline stocks are roughly 9 million barrels short of the threshold Beijing wants restored before allowing exports to normalize.
China had significantly increased exports during the summer. Official customs data showed total oil-product exports reached 6.01 million tonnes in August, up 12.7% year-on-year and the highest since March 2024, according to S&P Global. At the time, Chinese refiners said Beijing had not yet restricted clean-product exports despite tightening domestic supply.
The reversal comes as global diesel supplies are already being squeezed by Middle Eastern disruptions and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries. S&P Global warned this week that Asian fuel markets have limited surplus supply, meaning any further restriction on U.S. diesel exports would increase competition for Asian and Middle Eastern barrels.
China’s own government has meanwhile intervened to limit the domestic impact of high international oil prices, partially suppressing scheduled gasoline and diesel price increases in September while instructing refiners to ensure stable supplies.

articles.content_orig:
“ Primetime ” is a box office overachiever , but the subject of the A24 film calls it a “complete work of fiction.”
Lance Oppenheim’s movie centers on “To Catch a Predator,” the popular “Dateline” segment that ran from 2004 to 2007. In the show, an advocacy group with adult decoys posing as children would chat with online predators in order to lure them to a house, ostensibly to have sex with a minor. But instead of their prey, they would be met by host Chris Hansen (played by Robert Pattinson), who would interrogate the predators about why they were pursuing illicit and illegal affairs. The suspects were then arrested by law enforcement waiting outside the house.
The film is based more specifically on the 2009 Esquire article “Tonight on ‘Dateline’ This Man Will Die,” which chronicled an episode of the show involving Louis William Conradt Jr., an assistant district attorney in Murphy, Texas, who died by suicide after being caught in a police sting conducted in coordination with the “Predator” team.
Hansen is continuing his work on his media platform, TruBlu , which hosts shows such as the spiritual successor to “Predator,” “Takedown With Chris Hansen,” which launched in 2022.
Variety spoke with Hansen a few days after he watched “Primetime.” He discussed his perspective on its box office success, which parts are most upsetting to his former colleagues and what legal action he might take against A24.
No. The only elements of the movie that are not fictionalized are the fact that he uses my name and two or three catchphrases. Everything else is fictionalized. Yes, there was an assistant DA who tragically took his own life, but the circumstances surrounding it, the timeline, the events, it may be based on reality, but none of it is truthful. It’s a complete work of fiction.
Look, nobody wants to see somebody take their own life. But in this case, you had a public official, an assistant district attorney who prosecuted criminal cases, who, according to the police and evidence gathered in the case, conducted sexually explicit conversations with decoys posing as two different teenage boys. In Texas, like many other states, that constitutes a felony. Now, he didn’t show up at the house, but the police made a decision to get a warrant based on probable cause. And I think if you were to talk to the police making those decisions, they would tell you that there was some concern that evidence might be destroyed and that they were going to go serve that arrest warrant at his home.
Now, obviously, we knew they were gonna do this, and we captured the action from the street. And when they went in, according to Murphy police, he had a gun in his hand. He said, “I’m not going to hurt you guys,” and took his own life. Later, Texas Rangers did an investigation, and they determined that on that computer from which he was trying to extract the hard drive, there was child sexually abusive material. As a prosecutor, he knew that in Texas, you could potentially face 10 years in prison for each of those images. So nobody can tell you exactly why Bill Conradt took his own life. Nobody wanted to see it happen. It’s tragic for his family. It’s tragic for him. But to insinuate that there was some push on our part to go arrest him or get him or to find him or to cajole him, it just didn’t happen. He surfaced like any other alleged predator did in an investigation. The decoys don’t go try to find them. They conduct the investigation, and they find us.
The rules on it are very, very explicit. But we have caught a number of high-profile people. We were in San Francisco on a sting last month, and an Ivy League-educated lawyer who ran a multimillion-dollar investment fund showed up in the middle of the day to sexually exploit a 6- and 13-year-old boy whose father he thought was going to take part in the sex act. We don’t look for people; they find us. The whole premise of the movie is false. It’s a fake narrative. It didn’t happen. If that was the case and the police wanted to make a big splash publicitywise, wouldn’t you think they’d wait till Monday when he was sitting in his office at the district attorney’s office and barge in and get him and walk him out of there? That’s what they would have done. Everybody wants to say that this was done for clicks and ratings, and it wasn’t; it was just part of an investigation.
If anybody would take a moment, as some content creators have, and actually look at the story that we did on that particular case, and look at what we did on “The Today Show” the next morning, we were painstakingly transparent about what happened, how it happened and, as much as we knew, why it happened, as we have been with this franchise from the very beginning, continuing through today when we do these investigations which we now call “Takedown With Chris Hansen.” Any sense that anybody involved was pushing forward or that there was a ratings-hungry producer, none of that is true. Even the notion of the name of the film, “Primetime” — “Dateline” has always been on primetime television. It wasn’t like it was at 2 o’clock in the morning, and we were trying to get it on primetime. It was always on primetime. No discussion in that film ever happened.
There are people who think that we have historically worked too closely with law enforcement. But my argument is that’s the only way to be socially responsible and to ensure that there’s justice served in these cases. In the first two investigations, we didn’t collaborate with law enforcement. We didn’t know what was going to happen, but it became very clear in the third investigation that we needed to have a law enforcement presence. That has evolved over the past 22 years into what I think is the best possible way of doing this. That is to ensure justice and to ensure the chain of custody of evidence is secure. And also, look, it doesn’t matter how horrifying the crime is, everybody in this country is entitled to a vigorous defense. So the materials that we capture, obviously, everybody has access to that. Whether you’re the prosecutor or the defense, everybody deserves their fair day in court.
It’s par for the course. You know, even the filmmakers will tell you that this is fiction. And, you know, even when something reflects potentially a real-life event, the timeline has shifted around to make it work in the narrative of the filmmaker. But again, the timeline and the narrative and all of it is fiction. And so, the motives and everything that is detailed in the film, none of that actually happened the way it’s depicted. For them to do that, what’s the motive of making that film? A lot is being made of that right now. What does that say about Hollywood? If you’re gonna make a fictional film, why do you use my name?
The reason you use it is because I’ve spent 45 years creating a very valuable brand, and they wanted to exploit it. They know that if they use the name “Chris Hansen,” people will come to the movie. Most of them will understand the movie is fiction, and there’s a graphic at the end of the film saying so. But that’s not the way it’s portrayed in the beginning of the film. And because there was such an attempt to imitate — although I think it was way more dramatic and over the top — my mannerisms and my lines and things I’ve said over the years, they turned it into a science fiction film, almost, with the greens and the vampire look of the character. It’s just over the top. In fact, it was so over the top, I was left wondering, “What’s the point of this?” And again, I’m not objective, because they exploited me and my brand and my name image for commercial enterprise. articles.title_orig: The family of Renee Good files lawsuits over her death during Minneapolis ICE raids
articles.title_zh: The family of Renee Good files lawsuits over her death during Minneapolis ICE raids
articles.content_orig:
The family of Renee Good, from left; father Tim Ganger, mother Donna Ganger, brother Luke Ganger and brother Brent Ganger, listen during a news conference after the family sued the U.S. government and several immigration officials, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Minneapolis. Ellen Schmidt/AP hide caption
The family of Renee Good , the 37-year-old killed last January by a federal agent during the Trump administration's immigration enforcement surge in Minnesota, filed two civil lawsuits against the federal government Thursday.
One of the lawsuits, against the United States government itself, is essentially a wrongful death case, arguing that Jonathan Ross, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who killed Good, violated his agency's own policies and the Fourth Amendment by using excessive force.
It is seeking damages for Good's family for the suffering she experienced in the final moments of her life. And also for her partner, Becca Good, who witnessed the killing. The lawsuit says she has suffered intense emotional distress from what she has experienced. Ross shot Renee Good several times in her car. At the time, federal officials claimed she had weaponized her vehicle, though video evidence contradicted that.
The other lawsuit is rarer, alleging that federal officials engaged in a conspiracy to interfere with the civil rights of people in Minnesota.
It argues that Good's death was the "predictable and intended product" of the immigration crackdown in the state and that Ross' actions were in furtherance of a "carefully planned, coordinated effort" to make Somali and Hispanic people the "object of aggression and abduction" and to silence the people "who observed, documented, and warned of that campaign."
In making that argument, the lawyers, with the firm Romanucci & Blandin, relied on the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871, which was used to combat the terrorism wrought by the KKK during the Reconstruction era.
"I would say the second lawsuit is very unusual," Rachel Moran, a law professor at the University of St. Thomas, told NPR. "It was immediately striking to me because the Trump administration has been aggressively using conspiracy charges , including here in Minnesota, against people involved in protesting the administration's immigration tactics."
Moran said the lawyers in the Good lawsuits seem to be "turning that tactic on its head" by arguing that administration officials are involved in an illegal conspiracy themselves.
According to Ben Berkman, one of the lawyers representing Good's family, the first lawsuit is about what federal officers did to Renee Good on a Minneapolis street last winter. The second is about why those officers were on that street in the first place.
"It reaches the agent who fired those shots at Renee and it reaches every official who put him on the street that day," Berkman said. "No mask, no badge and no title in the administration puts anyone above that law."
Those federal officials include Ross, but also White House adviser Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, White House Border czar Tom Homan, and former Border Patrol Commander Gregory Bovino, among others. NPR reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment, but did not hear back.
In a statement, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said, "We intend to vigorously defend these baseless civil lawsuits."
The lawsuit also lists 10 federal agents who were also present at the scene as John Does, noting that the federal government has not released their identities and that they were wearing masks at the time of the killing.
The civil charges also underscore a lack of criminal charges . DHS has provided little public indication that it is investigating Good's death or the death of Alex Pretti at the hands of Border Patrol agents a few weeks later in Minneapolis. According to The Trace, a news site that focuses on gun violence, nine people have been killed by immigration agents since President Trump took office again last year.
A memorial for Renee Good, who was killed by federal agents in Minneapolis in January, remains in place at the site of her death, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Minneapolis. Ellen Schmidt/AP hide caption
At the state level in Minnesota, local officials have also not filed charges or released the findings of any investigation. In a statement, a spokesperson for Hennepin County, where Minneapolis is located, told NPR that state and local officials are reviewing the evidence and that they will "communicate transparently when a decision is reached."
At the press conference held Thursday, Good's family seemed frustrated at the inaction on all levels. Civil suits, like the ones filed by the family today, have the potential to hold entire institutions accountable rather than just individual actors.
"The fact that there's been no accountability, no investigation, no expression of condolence, no change in policy is completely mind-blowing," Brent Ganger, Good's brother, said. "We will not wait any longer. The time is absolutely now for accountability, for the deep damage done by ICE and others. We will not be quiet. We will not go away."
Brent and his mother, Donna Ganger, also testified before Congress last week at a hearing about fatal shootings by federal immigration officers.
In her first public appearance since the killing, Becca Good, Renee Good's partner, also spoke. She focused her words on who Renee was to her, calling her kind and loving, but also on what she has lost. Renee Good had three children, and Becca is still raising their youngest, a 6-year-old.
"This past August, I got ready to put our son in first grade. I bought him new shoes and a backpack and notebooks, pencil case, the whole nine yards. I went to Back To School Night on my own," Becca Good said. "She never missed a single moment. And this Halloween, it's our son's absolute favorite holiday. I'll take him trick or treating, without her hand in mine."

articles.title_zh: Disney’s Dana Walden on Jimmy Kimmel’s Late Night Future: “It’s Challenging”
articles.content_orig:
Television Business Editor
Dana Walden joked at the beginning of her Bloomberg Screentime session Thursday that her job was to “keep this seat warm for Casey Bloys, who’s bringing the real news.”
Disney’s president and chief creative officer stuck to that promise when asked about the future of Jimmy Kimmel Live! Kimmel signed a one-year contract extension in December 2025 to keep hosting the late night show through the 2026-27 season, and Bloomberg’s Lucas Shaw asked Walden if the host would be sticking around.
“I’m not going to make that announcement here with you today,” Walden said. “Again, I’m letting Casey make the news.” (Bloys, the head of HBO and HBO Max, is the presumptive front-runner to head up streaming at the combined Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery when that megamerger closes in the coming days.)
Speculation about Jimmy Kimmel Live! ‘s future has swirled since an early September Page Six story claimed Kimmel’s contract wouldn’t be renewed. ABC quickly denied that was the case, but other reports said the network is looking for significant budget cuts to keep the show going.
“The truth is, it’s a very challenging daypart,” Walden said Thursday at the Bloomberg event. “That’s not to say that Jimmy is not doing a phenomenal job, and his ratings are up. But they’re up relative to a smaller audience that’s watching late night on broadcast television.”
Kimmel and the show also have a big presence on YouTube and social media platforms, but those views and clicks bring in a fraction of the revenue that on-air advertising does. “That is not a lucrative opportunity for a very premium talk show,” said Walden.
“We’re trying to make sense of the business while also honoring a deep partnership,” she continued. “I love Jimmy; we have great friendship. He’s close to a number of the people at Disney. We’re trying to work through it and make sense of, what does Jimmy want, what’s the right thing to do, and what’s the right thing for our business.”

Sony’s new Quick Spectral Super Resolution AI upscaling is coming first to Marvel’s Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei.
Sony is launching a new AI upscaling technology specifically for the regular PS5. The new tech, called Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR), is a “new performance tier of AI upscaling” that’s a result of Sony’s Project Amethyst work with AMD, according to a blog post .
Sony says that PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR), which is available on the PS5 Pro , “remains the gold standard,” and in Digital Foundry ’s early hands-on with the tech , it does seem that QSSR isn’t as fast as PSSR because the PS5 doesn’t have dedicated machine learning silicon. As a result, you should probably expect closer to an upscaled 1440p resolution on PS5 instead of the upscaled 4K on PS5 Pro.
”On PS5 Pro, developers almost uniformly output to 4K and adjust render resolution beneath it,” Sony principal graphics R&D engineer Daniel Craig told Digital Foundry . “On PS5, teams have to be more flexible, tuning not just render resolution, but also their intermediate and final presentation targets depending on the graphics mode.”
But Craig also said that QSSR is “fundamentally a drop-in replacement for titles that already support PSSR” after only a few days of tuning, making it likelier that PS5 developers will take advantage. The tech will be “offered broadly to all PlayStation developers,” Sony says.
Marvel’s Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei will be the first games to take advantage of QSSR, and are getting patches today to offer the tech as “an additional graphics option on PS5.” ( Ghost of Yōtei Complete Edition also launches today .) Here are a couple videos from Sony showing off how QSSR looks in those games, and it appears to make graphics a little bit sharper:
Digital Foundry writes that “the potential here is remarkable: low resolution and poor upscaling have impacted so many titles in this generation, but QSSR could make a big difference.”

articles.title_orig: Whale sinks yacht in South Pacific causing military rescue mission
articles.title_zh: Whale sinks yacht in South Pacific causing military rescue mission
articles.content_orig:
A sperm whale cracked the hull of a yacht sailing in the remote South Pacific, forcing four sailors into a day-and-night fight for survival on the high seas.
Crew members on the 52-foot Tai Tam told AFP on Thursday of their weekend encounter with a pod of sperm whales 250 nautical miles north of tiny Norfolk Island.
"There was sort of a loud thud. The whole boat was pushed sideways," said Australian Jemma Cooper, who was thrown from the steering wheel by the force of the blow.
Not knowing at first what had happened, she noticed a brown discoloration in the water and a sperm whale.
"We looked out to our port side, and there were six to eight, a pod, of whales there. So then it became clear that that's what it was," she told AFP.
Her husband Jeremy Cooper said he was sleeping below deck when the impact woke him.
"It was pretty immediately evident it was very serious," he said.
"All the steering gear was smashed on the starboard side, and there was a significant amount of water coming in," Jeremy told AFP.
At 1 p.m. New Zealand time on Saturday — about 30 minutes after the whale collision — they activated an emergency beacon.
"We declared a full mayday," said New Zealand crew member Terry Hetherington, adding they spent the next few hours bailing out as much water as they could.
The Royal New Zealand Air Force flew a P-8A Poseidon patrol plane to the area to establish radio communications and coordinate the rescue, the military said in a news release , which included images of the rescue.
French crew member Martin Jaffre said the whale collision left several gashes in the hull and cracked the fiberglass structure, as well as breaking the steering.
"We could no longer steer the boat, and a boat with no steering quickly becomes a problem," he told AFP.
Jaffre battled to slow the incoming water with anything to hand, including expansion foam, and swam below the boat to inspect the hull, his crewmates said.
The sailors tried to stay aboard as long as possible, struggling to stop the engine getting clogged and bailing by hand.
Late at night, they abandoned the boat and transferred to a life raft in calm seas and under a full moon.
In the early hours of Sunday morning, they cut the tether to the yacht, fearing it might drag them down. Soon after, it slipped beneath the waves.
The New Zealand military released dramatic drone video of the yacht plunging below the water's surface and the crew ultimately being rescued.
A 470-foot container ship, the MV Sofrana Surville, rescued the sailors at 6 a.m. on Sunday, the New Zealand military said — about 18 hours after their encounter with the sperm whale.
Even the rescue was scary as the giant ship approached their tiny life raft, recalled Jeremy Cooper.
But within half an hour they had scaled a ladder to join their rescuers, have a cup of coffee and chat with the captain, he said, ruing the end of their Pacific holiday voyage.
"It was wonderful, wonderful, and just a terrible, terrible ending — but luckily no loss of life."
Rescue Coordination Centre Operations Manager Mike Clulow praised the efforts of the rescue team and the yacht's crew.
"This was a well-coordinated and executed rescue," Clulow said. "The crew of the yacht did all the right things, and it was unfortunate to have struck a whale in open water. They were well prepared and the early activation of their EPIRB (Emergency Position-Indicating Radio Beacon) was key to helping get them to safety. It is an excellent reminder that being prepared when going to sea can save your life."
Adult male sperm whales measure between 50 and 60 feet. They are considered a "vulnerable" species by the nonprofit International Union for Conservation of Nature. Sperm whales reproduce once every five to seven years and have experienced significant population decline. The species is under threat from noise pollution, plastic consumption and ship strikes.
The incident in New Zealand marks at least the second time in less than two months that a whale has sunk a boat. In July, a whale that surfaced for air slammed into a New Jersey fire department's boat, sinking the ship with firefighters on board.  Someone on a personal watercraft nearby and a boater helped rescue the firefighters from the water.

articles.title_orig: Mortgage Rates Surge, Notching Largest Weekly Gain in Four Years
articles.title_zh: Mortgage Rates Surge, Notching Largest Weekly Gain in Four Years
articles.content_orig:
Mortgage rates keep going up.
The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 7.28% this week, up from 7.03% last week, according to Freddie Mac data released Thursday. Mortgage rates have risen for six straight weeks, and this week brought the biggest one-week jump in nearly four years. Rates are now at their highest level since November 2023.
Turmoil in the bond market is driving rates higher. The 10-year Treasury yield has risen in recent months as investors worry that the Iran war and increased government spending could further stoke inflation and push the Federal Reserve toward higher rates for longer.
If you’re currently in the market for a home, the good news is you may be facing less competition from rate-sensitive buyers who are stepping back. But if you need a mortgage, the bad news is you will likely pay more in monthly costs than you would have just a few months ago.
But even with borrowing costs high – and potentially headed higher – a sub-7% mortgage rate may still be within reach for some buyers. The trade-off could be a riskier loan or a much bigger upfront payment.
Most home buyers opt for a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage because it typically offers lower monthly payments and predictable costs.
But it’s not the only option. Other types of mortgages may offer lower interest rates, potentially saving borrowers money over the life of the loan.
A 15-year mortgage typically has a lower interest rate than a 30-year mortgage, though monthly payments are significantly higher. Another option that is becoming increasingly popular lately: adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs).
As of the latest data last week, “ARM loans, with rates around 80 basis points lower than fixed rate loans, accounted for 10.3% of applications, the highest share since October 2025,” according to Joel Kan, deputy chief economist at the Mortgage Bankers Association.
How are higher interest rates and rising prices affecting you?
But ARM loans, the mortgage products that helped fuel housing market risk in the lead-up to the 2008 financial crisis, are riskier than fixed-rate loans . They typically offer a lower fixed rate for five, seven or 10 years before resetting with market rates. If rates are higher when the fixed period ends, borrowers can be hit with sharply higher monthly payments.
“It may work well for some borrowers who are expecting to move or refinance in four or five years,” said Jeremy Luke, a divisional director at Chase Home Lending. “It may not work for all.”
Another way to get a lower mortgage rate is to take over someone’s existing mortgage as an assumable loan .
Not all home loans can be passed to a home buyer, but most government-backed loans, such as those from the Federal Housing Administration, the US Department of Veterans Affairs and the US Department of Agriculture, are assumable.
However, the approval process for an assumable mortgage can take longer. And because the buyer takes over only the seller’s remaining loan balance, they may need to bring significantly more cash to the table to cover the difference between that balance and the home’s purchase price.
The rate an individual buyer gets depends on more than market conditions. Lenders also consider factors such as the borrower’s credit score, debt-to-income ratio and down payment, said Jeff DerGurahian, head economist at loanDepot.
After shopping around, if you are unsatisfied with the rates you’ve been offered, it’s often possible to pay more up front in exchange for a reduced interest rate.
Permanent buydowns lower your interest rate for the life of the loan, whereas temporary buydowns, which can be cheaper, lower your rate for only the first few years.
But it’s important not to overdo it, DerGurahian said.
“You don’t want to put so much money down that you can’t do what you need to do to live in your house and live day-to-day,” he said.
Sometimes, the home’s seller or a builder can cover the cost of a rate buydown.
Builders are leaning more heavily on incentives to attract buyers to new construction, offering concessions such as mortgage rate buydowns and closing-cost credits. In September, 66% of builders reported using sales incentives, up from 63% in August and the highest share since December, according to the National Association of Home Builders’ sentiment survey.
A buyer should also understand the demand picture in their local market, said DerGurahian.
If it’s a buyer’s market, that means the supply of homes in that area exceeds demand, giving home buyers the upper hand. If a homeowner is motivated to sell, they may be willing to offer concessions to attract a buyer. If sellers have the upper hand in a local market, though, it’s less likely.
Certain buyers may have access to federal programs that can help them secure more favorable mortgage rates, including VA loans for eligible veterans and USDA loans for buyers purchasing homes in qualifying rural areas.
There are also banks and credit unions that offer relationship pricing or preferential rates.
For example, Chase occasionally runs “rate sales” where home buyers (and homeowners looking to refinance) can lock in discounted rates, Luke said.
Some banks, including Chase, also offer a discounted rate if customers move eligible deposits and investments into that bank, Luke added.
It pays to shop around. Experts generally recommend applying with at least three different mortgage lenders to make sure you’re getting a competitive rate. Compare the rates offered, closing costs and other fees to get a clearer picture of the total cost of each loan.
And you don’t necessarily have to worry about multiple credit checks dinging your score. To shop around for mortgages without hurting your credit, limit your search to a window of 14 to 45 days, according to Bankrate.

Paramount has agreed to set up a board to keep tabs on the independence of its news properties as part of its recent settlement with a set of state attorneys general who wanted to block its deal. The Wall Street Journal previously reported on the talks between Paramount and the executive.

They are also concerned about the direction Paramount may see for CNN’s new streaming service. CNN’s progress with digital audiences has been slowed by a bevy of changes in the company’s corporate direction in recent years.
Thompson last week expressed a desire to stay in the role. “I am enthusiastic about staying,” he told employees during a recent town hall meeting, according to two people with knowledge of his remarks. Even so, he also confided he has no knowledge of how Paramount Skydance wanted to proceed once it completes its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery.
“How Paramount wants to run news” is not known to him at present, he said.
During his tenure, Thompson has focused on getting CNN content in front of younger viewers and digital audiences. articles.title_zh: Winner of Nikon microscopy photo contest faces criticism over AI usage
articles.content_orig:
The organizers of a highly regarded scientific photography contest are reviewing this year’s winning entry following criticism over the use of AI.
Nikon has announced that it’s “carefully re-reviewing the information” provided by Ning Xu, whose short video of intricate cell movement won the annual Small World In Motion competition in September.
At the time, Xu was a researcher at Tsinghua University in China. He’s since joined National University of Singapore as a research fellow, according to Nikon .
In a post on LinkedIn on Saturday, Nikon said that, “Xu is respectfully complying and has provided detailed technical documentation outlining the microscopy equipment, imaging methods, and processing techniques used to create the source video.”
Astonishing footage of abnormal cell movement in lungs wins 2026 Nikon video microscopy prize
The video captures the abnormal beating of airway cilia — hairlike structures that protrude from cells within the human body — in a child living with primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD), a rare genetic disorder, Nikon said at the time the winner was revealed.
In mid-September, Nikon announced that the video, which was created using an advanced microscopic imaging tool, had won the 16th annual Nikon Small World in Motion competition.
Last week, the competition posted the video on LinkedIn, where it received a number of critical comments from other users.
Edward Phelps, an associate professor at the University of Florida, said there were “many serious problems with this video.” He said that some of the biological structures shown in the footage do not behave as expected. “The microscopy community deserves an explanation from Nikon,” Phelps added.
Ian Donovan, a PhD student at UT Southwestern Medical Center, wrote that the video has “an embedded SynthID watermark identifying synthetic/AI-generated content.”
Xu replied to some of the criticism on Nikon’s LinkedIn post, saying that “AI was not used to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion.”
“It was applied afterwards to the reconstructed grayscale data to distinguish and color structures with similar morphology,” he added.
“A more detailed description of the optical system and quantitative analysis of the ciliary motion are currently being prepared for publication, and we hope to make these available soon,” he said.
“For me, the important distinction is between using an image to make a scientific claim and using visualization to communicate the beauty of scientific data,” added Xu. “Both can have a place, as long as we are clear about which is which.”

LONDON — He was one of my most memorable interviews. Even though we were both speaking English, I could barely understand a word he was saying.
"The costermongers, wheeze used to fly-pitch, on this frog and toad," he said — at least I think, after listening to my tape several times again, none the wiser.
Our interview was back in 2016, on one of my first NPR reporting trips to London. George Major, then 78, was a local celebrity. We walked together through the East End, where the factories and docklands that Major grew up around during World War II have given way to glass skyscrapers. A vendor ran out into the street to slap him high-five. Tourists snapped photos.
Major had turned up in bling: A black suit and flat cap, both festooned with sequins, sparkles and mother-of-pearl buttons. His title — Pearly King of Peckham — was spelled out in shimmering buttons across the back of his jacket.
He was a charming wheeler-dealer. But his language — a mix of what he called "backspeak" and Cockney rhyming slang — was impossible for this hapless American visitor to understand.
At one point in our video interview, I glanced at the camera and exclaimed, "We might need a translator here!"
Ten years later, I chuckle whenever I land at Heathrow Airport, where a portrait of Major covers an entire wall. But this summer, a former colleague alerted me to an item in the local press, which hit me harder than I expected: The Pearly King of Peckham died Aug. 1, aged 88.
He was buried Sept. 14 in a cemetery not far from the Cockney Museum he founded. A horse-drawn cart carried his casket into a little chapel, whose walls shook with mourners singing raucous pub songs. One of the gardeners outside looked bewildered.
At the gravesite, I approached the Major family, offered condolences, and hesitantly shared the story of my brief, confusing 2016 encounter with their loved one.
A horde of pearly kings, queens, princes and princesses — four generations of Major's family, all in matching pearly suits — turned and looked at me, some through tears, then threw back their heads and laughed.
"A real Cockney cheeky chappy!" his daughter Janet Major said, hugging me.
Pearly kings and queens, wearing clothes decorated with mother-of-pearl buttons, are committed to raising money for charities. Laura Chiesa/LightRocket viz Getty Images hide caption
In the 1870s, an orphaned street sweeper named Henry Croft began decorating his suit with mother-of-pearl buttons scavenged from the streets outside textile factories that used to dot London's East End.
His pearly garb infused menial work with dignity — a royal air, even — and launched what would become a working-class East London institution: The pearly kings and queens .
"These pearly suits are now cultural artifacts with fantastic designs, telling a profound story about London and Cockneys, what we call the non-posh Londoners," says Andy Green, co-founder of the Modern Cockney Festival, an annual celebration of diverse, working-class communities in London.
Some of the so-called pearlies were street hawkers, market vendors or fly-pitchers — unlicensed traders. Others canvassed for charity. Many were immigrants, their slang peppered with words from Yiddish or Bengali. They became neighborhood fixtures, in mother-of-pearl finery.
"You had what are called costermongers, which is a posh word for street hawkers, street sellers," Green says. "Imagine you're a newly arrived immigrant in the country. One of the first jobs you could possibly do might be to hustle, sell goods on the street."
That's what George Major did. Born in 1938 inside a military barracks in Peckham, southeast London, he was abandoned as a child, grew up in a workhouse , and found odd jobs in the local market as a teenager, his daughter Janet explains.
"Dad eventually became one of the costermonger kings that used to run market stalls," she says. "It was not an easy childhood, but he followed the ideals of Henry Croft. That was before the welfare state, when you had to help your friends, your neighbors, your community."
Janet Major describes the weekends of her childhood, with her father leading all seven of his children, walking door to door in matching pearly suits, asking for money for charity.
Nowadays, a dwindling number of pearlies still canvass for charities like children's hospitals, women's shelters and veterans groups. They appear at summertime street festivals and march in parades.
George Major later trained as a plumber and ran a plumbing supply shop, she says.
Onscreen, the pearly kings inspired the streetwise, heart-of-gold chimney sweep character of Bert in Walt Disney's Mary Poppins film — played by Dick Van Dyke, an American who later owned up to what he called "the most atrocious Cockney accent in the history of cinema."
The Major family and others believe George Major himself inspired another fictional character: Del Boy , the happy-go-lucky East London huckster in the long-running British sitcom Only Fools and Horses . He's a cheeky salesman, always scheming to get rich quick, with the catchphrase, "This time next year, we'll be millionaires!"
At his funeral, Major's eulogy was riddled with Del Boy quotes.
But like the TV protagonist, Major also broke the law. In 2012 he was sentenced to six months in prison, after pleading guilty to benefits fraud . He was released early.
"If he could avoid the tax man, he would!" his daughter laughs. "He used to say, 'Discount for cash!' He'd love a bargain."
His fame overshadowed his legal troubles. Major was one of dozens of pearly royals who marched in the opening ceremony of the 2012 London Olympics.
George Major, seen here in 1975, was born in 1938 inside a military barracks in Peckham, southeast London, and grew up in a workhouse before he became the best-known pearly king of his generation. Chris Moorhouss/Hulton Archive via Getty Images hide caption
Years later, I finally figured out what Major meant back in 2016 when he told me he was a "costermonger" (street hawker) who used to "fly-pitch" (sell stuff without a license) on the "frog and toad" where we did our interview.
In Cockney rhyming slang, "frog and toad" means road. "Porky pies" means lies. "Apples and pears" means stairs. "Whistle and flute" means suit. "Ruby Murray" means curry. The vocabulary is extensive, and bewildering to outsiders — which is precisely the point. Green, the Cockney expert, says this type of slang likely originated as a code to confuse the police, or to secretly rig prices among street vendors.
To complicate things, Major also spoke in what he called "backspeak," sometimes also called backslang, which is even more confusing. One example that's crept into mainstream British slang is the word "yob" for boy. Take any word at all, and simply spell it backwards.
One of the only parts of that 2016 interview I could understand at the time was when Major waxed poetic about his family's unique pearly suit pattern. He pointed to a row of buttons on his sleeve, calling them "the line of life."
Ten years later, at his funeral, I found myself examining the same pattern on a pearly outfit worn by his great-granddaughter.
"There's a straight line, which is your life line," Aleisha Gordon, 19, said, pointing to a row of shimmering buttons. "The triangles are the ups and downs in life, and the flowers are the friends and family that help you along the way."
After the funeral, children threw handfuls of earth as George Major's coffin was lowered into the ground. The undertaker brought out four caged doves for Major's descendants to release skyward. The birds circled twice overhead, then disappeared.
People shared anecdotes about a "real rascal" and "the most hilarious person" who was nevertheless "very particular" about who made his tea. Someone turned on a boombox, and mourners began kicking their legs

articles.title_orig: Willson Contreras Shades Red Sox's Use of Analytics in Video After Sonny Gray's Early Exit
articles.title_zh: Willson Contreras Shades Red Sox's Use of Analytics in Video After Sonny Gray's Early Exit
articles.content_orig:
Willson Contreras indicated he felt overuse of analytics led Boston Red Sox manager Chad Tracy to pull Sonny Gray from Wednesday's Wild Card round elimination loss after just 70 pitches against the New York Yankees.
Contreras initially responded to reporters asking about his reaction to Gray's fifth-inning exit from the 9-2 loss by miming zipping his lips before elaborating.
"It's not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers that are telling you what to do, because this is baseball," Contreras said (h/t SNY). "The data is here to help us, but at the end of the day, you're going to have to need experience and veteran guys to win games."
When asked if he felt the Red Sox relied too much on data, Contreras nodded as he said, "If you watch the game."
Tracy, who had also pulled Game 1 starter Payton Tolle early, called Gray off the mound with two runners on base, one out remaining and the Red Sox trailing by one run in the bottom of the fifth.
Gray was replaced by Erik Miller, who on his third pitch of the game allowed a two-RBI single from Cody Bellinger.
Tracy then turned to Garrett Crochet for the sixth inning. Crochet allowed a run and loaded the bases until he was removed for Garrett Whitlock, who allowed five more runs before he was able to close out the frame.
Tracy said after the elimination loss he used the same reasoning to pull Gray as he had to remove Tolle from a Game 1 shutout loss to the Yankees.
"We're trailing. We're struggling to score runs, and when you get into spots where you're struggling to score runs and you're already trailing, you feel like you've got to be aggressive," Tracy told reporters Wednesday night.
The Yankees will now advance to face the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS, while the Red Sox will concede their second Wild Card loss in as many years. Ranger Suárez, who was slated to start a potential deciding Game 3, will not pitch this postseason.
The Red Sox fired former manager Alex Cora and turned to Tracy following a 10-17 start to the season. Tracy lost his interim tag and inked a three-year extension after leading the club to clinch a postseason berth.
Tracy will now be tasked with helping his club find a way to respond next fall to scoring two runs across their two postseason games.
